summary.text: Spiral galaxies are a class described by Edwin Hubble, with a flat rotating disk of stars, gas and dust and a central bulge of stars.
Their spiral arms are sites of ongoing star formation and shine brighter than the surrounding disc because of the young, hot OB stars that live in them.
Roughly two-thirds of spirals have a bar from whose ends the arms begin, and the Milky Way is a barred spiral.

facts.label: Bars over time
facts.value: From about 10% eight billion years ago to over two-thirds now

facts.label: Where they live
facts.value: Mostly low-density regions, rare in cluster centers

facts.label: Bulge black holes
facts.value: Many bulges are thought to host a supermassive black hole

items.prompt: A spiral galaxy's arms look brighter than the disc around them. What is responsible?

options.label: Dust that reflects the light of the galaxy's oldest stars
Young, hot stars that live in the arms
A bright ring of stars around the black hole
The galaxy's halo shining through the disc

items.explain: The arms are brighter than the surrounding disc because of the young, hot OB stars that inhabit them.

items.prompt: An astronomer describes a spiral galaxy with loosely wound arms and a small bulge of young, blue stars. Which Hubble type is it?

options.label: Type Sa or SBa
Type Sc or SBc
Either, since arm tightness does not vary
Neither, since these traits belong to ellipticals

items.explain: Sc and SBc galaxies have very loose arms and smaller bulges of young, blue Population I stars.

items.prompt: Most stars in a spiral galaxy orbit in a plane, following roughly circular paths. A few follow tilted, backward or irregular paths and only occasionally pass through that plane. Where do those stars belong?

options.label: In the spiral arms
In the thin layer of dust in the disc
In the halo around the galaxy
In the disk of gas around the central black hole

items.explain: Some stars inhabit a spheroidal halo, where orbits may be retrograde, highly inclined, or irregular, and they sometimes pass through the disc.

items.prompt: Eight billion years ago, how common were bars among spiral galaxies compared with now?

options.label: About the same share as today
Much more common, since bars fade with age
Far less common, with only about 10% barred
Equally common as barless ones, at about half

items.explain: Only about 10% of spirals had bars about 8 billion years ago, compared with over two-thirds now.

items.prompt: Where in the universe are spiral galaxies mostly found?

options.label: In low-density regions, rare in cluster centers
At the centers of the densest galaxy clusters
Only far away from any other galaxy at all
Evenly spread everywhere, with no pattern to it

items.explain: Spirals are mostly found in low-density regions and are rare in the centers of galaxy clusters.

items.prompt: Astronomers call the Milky Way a barred spiral, yet picking out its bar is hard. Why?

options.label: The bar is too dim to detect
Earth sits within the galactic disc
The bar is hidden by a nearby galaxy
The bar only appears every few million years

items.explain: The bar is difficult to observe from Earth's current position within the galactic disc.

paragraphs.heading: Disks with arms
paragraphs.text: Spiral galaxies are a class that Edwin Hubble described in his 1936 work The Realm of the Nebulae, which makes them part of the Hubble sequence. Most have a flat, spinning disk of stars, gas and dust around a central crowd of stars called the bulge. Around these there is often a much fainter halo of stars, many of them in globular clusters. The galaxies take their name from the spiral patterns that reach from the center out into the disk.

paragraphs.heading: The spiral arms
paragraphs.text: The spiral arms are long, thin regions of stars curving out from the center. They are where new stars keep forming, and they shine brighter than the rest of the disk because of the young, hot stars living in them. Those stars are blue, and there are many of them. Arm shapes differ by class: Sc and SBc galaxies have loose arms, while Sa and SBa galaxies have tightly wrapped ones.

paragraphs.heading: Bars
paragraphs.text: Roughly two-thirds of spirals have a bar-shaped band of stars running out from the bulge, and the spiral arms begin at its ends. A bar can be strong or weak. Bars have likely become more common: about 8 billion years ago only around 10% had them, roughly a quarter did 2.5 billion years ago, and today over two-thirds do. The Milky Way is a barred spiral, though the bar is hard to see from Earth's position inside the disk. The best evidence for it comes from several surveys, including one with the Spitzer Space Telescope.

paragraphs.heading: The halo
paragraphs.text: Not every star sits in the disk or bulge; some live in a round halo. The halo seems free of dust, and its stars are much older and lower in metals than those of the disk. Some halo stars come from small galaxies that fall in: the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy is merging with the Milky Way, and some stars in our halo were taken from it. Halo stars sometimes pass through the disk, and a few small red dwarfs near the Sun, such as Kapteyn's Star, are thought to belong to the halo.

paragraphs.heading: Where and how far back
paragraphs.text: Spirals and irregulars together make up about 60% of the galaxies in today's universe. Spirals tend to live in regions where galaxies are sparse, and are seldom found in the centers of galaxy clusters. They also go back a long way. As of 2024 the oldest and most distant known spiral is BRI 1335-0417, whose light took 12.4 billion years to reach Earth.
